learning_experiences: in pairs or groups, discuss and arrange real objects collected from the environment according to size starting with the smallest to the largest and from the largest to the smallest,
name the position of an object from a reference point using 1st, 2 nd up to 20 th ,

in groups of 20, race for a distance and assign each other the correct position using the words first, second up to twentieth position depending on when they finish the race. Write their positions in the race in symbols and in words,
in pairs/groups, relate numbers 1 to 20 to positions first, second up to 20 th and relate to real life situations. For example, birth order in a family; 1 st born, 2 nd born,
play games involving position 1 to 20 using digital devices and other resources.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we tell our positions in a competition?
sub_strands.design_notes: Outcomes a to c are KICD's words; d is attitudinal. Grade 3 number concept is about size order and ordinal positions 1st to 20th, said and written in symbols (1st) and words (first).

skills.name: Order objects according to size
skills.mastery: The child arranges three to six real objects or pictures from the smallest to the largest and from the largest to the smallest, says which is first and last in the order, and keeps to the size asked for (length, height or bulk), not colour or position.
question_forms: order pictures from smallest to largest
which comes first or last in the order
which object is out of order

prerequisites.reason: Represents numbers with objects, so compares amounts and sizes.

skills.hands_on: Arranging real objects collected from the school compound is done in class.

skills.name: Identify the position of objects from 1st to 20th
skills.mastery: Given a line of up to 20 objects or people and a reference point (the front, the left), the child names the position of any one of them (the 7th) and points to the one in a named position, counting from the stated end.
question_forms: which position is the object in
point to the object in a position
who is just before or after

prerequisites.reason: Has put objects in order, so a line has a first and a last.

skills.name: Write positions in number symbols and in words
skills.mastery: The child writes a position from 1st to 20th in symbols (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th ... 20th) with the right ending, and in words (first, second, third, twelfth, twentieth) with the right spelling, and matches the two forms.

prerequisites.reason: Knows the positions before writing them.
Reads and writes numbers 1 to 20 in words.

misconceptions.error: Orders from largest to smallest when asked for smallest to largest.

example.question: Put these sticks from the shortest to the longest: 8 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm.

misconceptions.cause: Does not attend to the direction words.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 8, 5, 3 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Point to the start and say 'shortest first'; place the first object before the others.

misconceptions.error: Keeps the objects in the order they were shown, or in the order they lie on the table.

example.question: A bottle, a cup and a jerrycan are shown in that order. Order them from smallest to largest.

misconceptions.cause: Reads the order of the picture as the order of size.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer bottle, cup, jerrycan as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Compare two at a time by holding them side by side.

misconceptions.error: Compares the tops of objects that do not start at the same line.

example.question: Two pencils: one starts further up the table. Which is longer?
example.correct_answer: the one that is longer from end to end

misconceptions.cause: Looks only at where the objects end.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the one that reaches higher as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Line up one end of every object first.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Finds the smallest and largest but puts the middle objects in any order.

example.question: Order from smallest to largest: 4 stones of different sizes.
example.wrong_answer: smallest, third largest, second largest, largest
example.correct_answer: smallest, second smallest, second largest, largest

misconceptions.cause: Compares only with the two ends.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer smallest, third largest, second largest, largest as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: After the first, choose the smallest of those left, again and again.

misconceptions.error: Counts the position from the wrong end of the line.

example.question: Ten children stand in a queue. Amina is 3rd from the front. How many children are in front of her?

misconceptions.cause: Counts from the back, or counts the children behind.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 7 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Mark the front with a flag and always start counting there.

misconceptions.error: Says the number of people in front is the same as the position.

example.question: Otieno is 5th in the line. How many people are in front of him?

misconceptions.cause: Counts Otieno himself among those in front.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 5 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Line up 5 children and count those in front of the 5th.

misconceptions.error: Loses the count past 10 and names the next position wrongly.

example.question: What position comes after 12th?

misconceptions.cause: Counts the positions too fast past ten.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 14th as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Touch each object and say each position aloud.

misconceptions.error: Answers with how many there are instead of the position.

example.question: There are 8 mangoes in a row. Which position is the last mango in?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes counting how many with naming a position.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 8 mangoes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask 'how many?' and 'which one?' as two questions.

misconceptions.error: Writes 'th' after every number, as 1th, 2th, 3th.

example.question: Write the position second in symbols.

misconceptions.cause: Learnt the 'th' ending and uses it for all.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2th as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show 1st, 2nd and 3rd as the three special endings; from 4th to 20th the ending is th.

misconceptions.error: Spells the irregular words as they sound, as twelveth, fiveth or nineth.

example.question: Write 12th in words.

misconceptions.cause: Adds -th to the counting word.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer twelveth as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: List the special spellings: fifth, ninth, twelfth.

misconceptions.error: Writes the counting word instead of the position word.

example.question: Write 3rd in words.

misconceptions.cause: Does not tell number words and position words apart.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer three as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Say 'the third child', 'three children' and hear the difference.

misconceptions.error: Writes a teen position with the digits reversed, as 41st for fourteenth.

example.question: Write fourteenth in symbols.

misconceptions.cause: Hears 'four' first and writes the 4 first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 41th as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Fourteen is ten and four: write the 1 for the ten first.

in pairs / groups, read numbers 1 to 1000 in symbols starting from any point,
in pairs and taking turns, read and write numbers 1 to 100 in words using number cards,
in pairs or groups, create number patterns up to 1000 and share with other groups,
play games involving whole numbers up to 1000 using digital devices and other resources.

How do you tell the place value of a digit in a number?

skills.name: Count forward up to 1,000 from any point
skills.mastery: Starting from any number up to 1,000, the child counts on in ones, tens or hundreds, crossing a ten or a hundred correctly (198, 199, 200; 390, 400, 410), and says the next three numbers.
question_forms: count on in ones from a number
what comes next after a hundred

prerequisites.reason: Sees which digit changes at a ten or hundred.

skills.name: Count backward in hundreds from 1,000
skills.mastery: The child counts back from 1,000 in hundreds (1,000, 900, 800 ... 100) and from any hundred, and says the hundred before a given hundred.
question_forms: missing hundred in a backward line

skills.name: Place value of digits up to hundreds
skills.mastery: For any number up to 999 the child names the place of each digit (hundreds, tens, ones), says what each digit is worth (the 4 in 347 is 40), builds the number from hundreds, tens and ones including an empty place (3 hundreds and 5 ones is 305), and compares numbers by their hundreds first.
question_forms: name the place of a digit
write hundreds, tens and ones as a number

prerequisites.reason: Place value in ones and tens.
Represents numbers with objects in groups of ten.

skills.name: Read numbers 1 to 1,000 in symbols
skills.mastery: The child reads aloud any number up to 1,000 written in symbols, saying the hundreds, the 'and' and the tens and ones (406 is four hundred and six), and picks the number said from a list.
question_forms: match a number to its name
read a price or a page number

prerequisites.reason: Knows the first digit of three is the hundreds.

skills.name: Read and write numbers 1 to 100 in words
skills.mastery: The child writes any number up to 100 in words with the correct spelling (forty, not fourty; a hyphen in twenty-seven) and writes a number given in words in symbols.
question_forms: write the words as a number

prerequisites.reason: Reads and writes numbers 1 to 20 in words.
Knows the tens and ones of a 2-digit number.

skills.name: Missing numbers in number patterns up to 1,000
skills.mastery: The child finds the rule of a pattern that goes up or down in ones, twos, fives, tens or hundreds (240, 250, 260, __), fills in missing numbers in the middle or at the end, and makes a pattern of their own. Number games with patterns are done in class.

prerequisites.reason: Counts on in tens and hundreds.

misconceptions.error: Does not cross the hundred: says 109 after 199, or 1000 after 199.
misconceptions.cause: Adds a zero or a one as when crossing a ten, without seeing the hundreds digit change.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 1000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Use an abacus: 199 plus one bead makes 10 tens into a new hundred.

misconceptions.error: Counting in tens past a hundred, writes 3100 or skips to 500.

example.question: Count on in tens: 380, 390, __

misconceptions.cause: Writes 39 tens plus one ten as 3 then 10.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3100 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count in tens on a hundred square: ten tens make the next hundred.

misconceptions.error: Counts the starting number again when counting on.

example.question: Count on 3 from 456. Where do you stop?

misconceptions.cause: Says the start number as 'one'.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 458 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put a finger on 456 and say 'one' only on the next step.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Counts on in ones when asked to count in tens.

example.question: Count on in tens from 520: 520, __

misconceptions.cause: Does not hear the size of the step.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 521 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Say the step before each jump: 'add ten'.

misconceptions.error: Counts forward when asked to count back.

example.question: Count back in hundreds: 700, 600, __

misconceptions.cause: Treats counting as always going up.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 700 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Walk backwards along a hundreds number line as you count.

misconceptions.error: After 1,000 says 9000 or 990 instead of 900.

example.question: Count back in hundreds from 1,000: 1000, __

misconceptions.cause: Takes away a ten, or writes the 9 in the wrong place.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 990 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show 1,000 as ten hundred bundles and remove one bundle.

misconceptions.error: Counts back in tens instead of hundreds.

example.question: Count back in hundreds: 400, 300, __

misconceptions.cause: Mixes the size of the step after a few numbers.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 290 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write each step on the line: minus 100.

misconceptions.error: Stops at 100 or says 'zero hundred' and cannot say the last step.

example.question: Count back in hundreds: 300, 200, 100, __

misconceptions.cause: Has not met 0 as the end of a count.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 00 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count back the bundles until none are left: zero.

misconceptions.error: Says a digit is worth only itself, whatever its place.

example.question: What is the 4 in 347 worth?

misconceptions.cause: Sees the digit, not the place.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put 347 in a place value chart and build it with bundles.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a zero when building a number with an empty place.

example.question: Write 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 5 ones as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks nothing need be written for no tens.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 35 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write in a three-column chart: every column gets a digit, 0 for empty.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the ones first, so the digits come out reversed.

example.question: Write 2 hundreds, 6 tens and 8 ones as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Writes in the order the digits are found, not the order of places.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 862 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Label the chart: hundreds on the left, ones on the right.

misconceptions.error: Adds the digits together instead of placing them.

example.question: Write 4 hundreds, 3 tens and 2 ones as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Treats 'and' as add the digits.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 9 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the bundles: 4 hundreds is 400, not 4.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out one of the places, so the number has too few digits or a zero where a digit belongs.

example.question: Write 5 hundreds, 7 tens and 1 one as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Loses track of the middle place.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 501 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Tick each place in the chart as its digit is written.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the number with the biggest digit anywhere is the greatest.

example.question: Which is greater, 189 or 312?

misconceptions.cause: Looks for the largest digit, 9, instead of the hundreds.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 189 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Compare the hundreds first: 1 hundred or 3 hundreds?

misconceptions.error: Reads the zero aloud, as 'four hundred zero six'.

example.question: Read 406 aloud.

misconceptions.cause: Says every digit it sees.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer four hundred zero six as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show 406 with bundles: no tens, so the word for tens is left out.

misconceptions.error: Reads the digits one by one, as 'two five three'.

example.question: Read 253 aloud.

misconceptions.cause: Has not learnt to name the places while reading.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer two five three as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Point to each digit and say its place before reading.

misconceptions.error: Reads a teen as a ty, as 'three hundred and forty' for 314.

example.question: Read 314 aloud.

misconceptions.cause: Fourteen and forty sound alike.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer three hundred and forty as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Build 314: 1 ten and 4 ones is fourteen, 4 tens is forty.

misconceptions.error: Says 'thousand' for a three-digit number.

example.question: Read 700 aloud.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks two zeros mean thousand.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer seven thousand as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the digits: three digits is hundreds, four digits is thousands.

misconceptions.error: Spells forty as fourty.

example.question: Write 40 in words.

misconceptions.cause: Spells it like four.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer fourty as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write four, fourteen, forty in a column and circle the missing u.

misconceptions.error: Writes a teen word for a ty number, as sixteen for 60.

example.question: Write 60 in words.

misconceptions.cause: The words sound alike.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sixteen as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Sixteen is 1 ten and 6; sixty is 6 tens.

misconceptions.error: Writes the number for a word with the digits reversed, as 72 for twenty-seven.

example.question: Write twenty-seven as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Writes the 7 heard in 'seven' first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 72 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Twenty is 2 tens: write the tens digit first.

misconceptions.error: Writes twenty-five as 205 or 20 5.

example.question: Write twenty-five as a number.

misconceptions.cause: Writes 20 then 5 side by side.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 205 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Twenty-five has 2 tens and 5 ones: two digits only.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds one each time when the pattern goes up in tens.
misconceptions.cause: Assumes every pattern goes up by one.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 261 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Find the jump between two numbers first: 250 minus 240.

misconceptions.error: Continues a falling pattern upwards.
misconceptions.cause: Does not check whether the numbers grow or shrink.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 800 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw arrows between terms and write + or -.

misconceptions.error: Uses only the first jump and misses that the jump changes or is in the middle.
misconceptions.cause: Fills the gap by adding one to the number before.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 111 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Check the jump on both sides of the gap.

misconceptions.error: Breaks the pattern when it crosses a hundred, as 480, 490, 4100.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the tens as 10 instead of moving to the next hundred.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4100 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count in tens on an abacus: ten tens is one hundred.

skills.name: Add a 3-digit number to a number of up to 2 digits without regrouping
skills.mastery: The child adds a 3-digit number and a 1- or 2-digit number with no carrying (342 + 25, 604 + 3), lining up ones under ones in a column and also working across, with sums up to 1,000. Practice with apparatus or digital games is done in class.
question_forms: a word story with a total
fill in the missing digit of the sum

skills.name: Add a 3-digit number to a number of up to 2 digits with single regrouping
skills.mastery: The child adds a 3-digit number and a 1- or 2-digit number where the ones (or the tens) make ten or more, carrying one ten (or one hundred) to the next column, as in 347 + 28 = 375, with the sum up to 1,000.
question_forms: find the mistake in a working

skills.name: Add two 3-digit numbers without regrouping
skills.mastery: The child adds two 3-digit numbers with no carrying (423 + 361), column by column from the ones, with a sum up to 1,000.

prerequisites.reason: Adds hundreds, tens and ones in columns.

skills.name: Add two 3-digit numbers with single regrouping
skills.mastery: The child adds two 3-digit numbers with one carry, from the ones to the tens or from the tens to the hundreds (256 + 318 = 574), with the sum up to 1,000, and writes the carried digit in the right column.

skills.name: Create and complete number patterns involving addition up to 1,000
skills.mastery: The child continues a pattern made by adding the same number each time (125, 150, 175, __), finds a missing term, names the number added, and makes a pattern of their own up to 1,000.

misconceptions.error: Lines up the 2-digit number under the hundreds and tens instead of the tens and ones.
misconceptions.cause: Writes both numbers from the left.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 592 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Line up from the right: ones under ones.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds the ones and copies the rest of the first number, forgetting the tens of the second.
misconceptions.cause: Stops after the ones column.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 537 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Tick each column of the smaller number as it is added.

misconceptions.error: Counts on from the first number and includes it, so the sum is one less.

example.question: 604 + 3, counting on

misconceptions.cause: Counts 604 as 'one'.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 606 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put a finger on 604 and count 605, 606, 607.

misconceptions.error: Writes the two numbers side by side, as 3425 for 342 + 5.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks 'add' means put next to.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3425 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show 342 bundles and 5 straws together: count them.

misconceptions.error: Writes the ones digit of the sum but forgets to carry the ten.
misconceptions.cause: Does not record the ten made.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 365 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Exchange 10 ones for a ten bundle and put it in the tens.

misconceptions.error: Writes the whole 2-digit sum of a column, as 3615 for 347 + 28.
misconceptions.cause: Does not see that a column holds one digit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3615 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: One digit per column: exchange the ten.

misconceptions.error: Carries the ten into the hundreds column.
misconceptions.cause: Puts the small 1 above the wrong digit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 393 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write the carried 1 directly above the tens.

misconceptions.error: Adds the carried one twice, or to two columns.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the carry above two digits.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 203 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Cross out the carried digit once you have added it.

misconceptions.error: Adds digits across columns, such as hundreds of one number with tens of the other.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the numbers out of line.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 748 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Use squared paper: one digit in each square.

misconceptions.error: Adds from the left and writes the digits in the wrong order.
misconceptions.cause: Starts with the hundreds and writes from the right.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 566 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Always start with the ones on the right and write under the column.

misconceptions.error: Takes the smaller digit from the larger in a column instead of adding.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the + and - signs.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 251 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Circle the sign and say 'add' before starting.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a zero in a column, so the sum is a 2-digit number.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks 0 + 0 means nothing to write.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 77 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Every column gets a digit, even 0.

misconceptions.error: Forgets to carry the ten from the ones.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the ones digit and moves on.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 564 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Exchange ten ones for one ten with bundles.

misconceptions.error: Takes away when the story says altogether.

example.question: A shop sells 245 eggs on Monday and 136 on Tuesday. How many altogether?

misconceptions.cause: Takes the smaller from the larger.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 109 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Altogether means put together: add.

misconceptions.error: Carries a ten that was not made, or carries twice.
misconceptions.cause: Carries out of habit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 588 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Carry only when a column makes 10 or more.

misconceptions.error: When the tens make ten or more, writes the 2-digit total in the tens column.
misconceptions.cause: Does not exchange ten tens for a hundred.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 5115 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ten tens make one hundred: carry it.

misconceptions.error: Adds one each time instead of the pattern's jump.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks a pattern goes up by one.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 176 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Find the difference between two terms first.

misconceptions.error: Uses a different jump for the next term.
misconceptions.cause: Guesses a round number.

example.question: The minute hand points to 8 and the hour hand is nearly at 5. What time?

misconceptions.cause: Does not see which half of the clock the hand is in.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 20 past 4 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw a line from 12 to 6: the right side is past, the left side is to.

misconceptions.error: Names the hour the short hand is moving to when it is past the hour.

example.question: The short hand is just after 4 and the long hand on 2. What time?

misconceptions.cause: Reads the nearest number to the short hand.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 10 past 5 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: For past, the hour is the number the short hand has just passed.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: For 'to' times, counts the minutes from 12 clockwise instead of to the 12.

example.question: The long hand points to 9. How many minutes to the hour?

misconceptions.cause: Counts forward from 12.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 45 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: For 'to', count from the minute hand on to 12.

misconceptions.error: Reads a digital time as one number, as 745 or 'seven hundred and forty-five'.

example.question: Read the digital clock 7:45.

misconceptions.cause: Ignores the colon.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer seven hundred and forty-five as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The colon splits hours from minutes.

misconceptions.error: Reads :45 as quarter past.

example.question: What is 3:45 on an analogue clock?

misconceptions.cause: Links 45 with a quarter but not with which quarter.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer quarter past 3 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: 45 minutes past is 15 minutes to the next hour.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads 4:05 as 4:50 or as 'four five past'.

example.question: What time is 4:05?

misconceptions.cause: Reads the 0 as nothing or swaps the digits.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer ten to five as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Minutes always have two digits: 05 is 5 minutes.

misconceptions.error: Gives the same hour for a 'to' time, as 6:40 = 20 to 6.

example.question: What is 6:40 in words?

misconceptions.cause: Keeps the hour shown instead of the next hour.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer twenty to six as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: 'To' counts towards the next hour.

misconceptions.error: Writes the number the hand points to instead of the minutes.

example.question: The long hand is on 5, the short hand just past 2. Write the time.

misconceptions.cause: Uses the clock number as the minutes.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer five past two as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.

misconceptions.error: Draws both hands the same length, or the hour hand on the hour number for a half-past time.

example.question: Draw half past 3.
example.correct_answer: short hand half way between 3 and 4

misconceptions.cause: Thinks the hour hand stays on the number.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer short hand exactly on 3 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Watch a real clock: the hour hand moves slowly between numbers.

misconceptions.error: Writes 'past' with the next hour, as 'twenty past five' for 4:20.

example.question: Write 4:20 in words.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes the hour used with past and to.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer twenty past five as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Past uses the hour just gone; to uses the next hour.

misconceptions.error: Writes 'thirty to' instead of half past.

example.question: Write the time when the long hand is on 6 and the short hand between 7 and 8.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the half-past name.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer thirty to eight as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: On 6 it is half way round: half past.

misconceptions.error: Gives an estimate far from real, such as 20 hours for a school day.

example.question: About how many hours is a school day?

misconceptions.cause: Has no feel for an hour.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 20 hours as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the hours from 8 o'clock to 3 o'clock on a clock.

misconceptions.error: Gives a short activity in hours.

example.question: About how long does it take to eat lunch?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes minutes and hours.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3 hours as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A lesson is less than an hour; lunch is shorter.

misconceptions.error: Says an activity takes less than an hour when it takes much more.

example.question: Does a night's sleep take more or less than an hour?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes more and less.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer less as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Think from going to bed to waking.

misconceptions.error: Orders activities by how much they are liked, not by time.

example.question: Put in order from shortest: a football match, brushing teeth, a school day.
example.wrong_answer: school day, football match, brushing teeth
example.correct_answer: brushing teeth, football match, school day

misconceptions.cause: Does not compare durations.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer school day, football match, brushing teeth as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask for each: minutes or hours?

misconceptions.error: Adds the hours to the minutes.

example.question: 2 h 15 min + 1 h 30 min

misconceptions.cause: Puts all the numbers in one column.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2 h 46 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Two columns: h and min. Add each on its own.

misconceptions.error: Writes the answer as one number, such as 345.

example.question: 2 h 15 min + 1 h 30 min

misconceptions.cause: Treats the time as a 3-digit number.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 345 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write h and min every time.

misconceptions.error: Adds the minutes and forgets the hours.

example.question: 1 h 20 min + 2 h 10 min

misconceptions.cause: Stops after one column.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 30 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Tick each column after adding it.

misconceptions.error: Subtracts when the story asks for total time.

example.question: A trip takes 2 h 10 min, then 1 h 20 min more. How long in all?

misconceptions.cause: Takes away because of the word more, wrongly.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 50 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: In all: add.

misconceptions.error: Takes minutes from hours.

example.question: 3 h 50 min - 1 h 20 min

misconceptions.cause: Lines up wrongly.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2 h 49 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Hours from hours, minutes from minutes.

misconceptions.error: Adds when asked how much longer.

example.question: A film lasts 2 h 40 min and a match 1 h 30 min. How much longer is the film?

misconceptions.cause: Longer sounds like more.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 h 10 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The extra time is the difference.

misconceptions.error: Finds how long from one o'clock time to another by counting the hour numbers, so gets one hour too many.

example.question: How long is it from 2 o'clock to 5 o'clock?

misconceptions.cause: Counts 2, 3, 4, 5 as four hours.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 hours as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the jumps between the numbers, not the numbers.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the time used instead of the time left.

example.question: A 3 h 40 min trip: 1 h 10 min done. How long is left?

misconceptions.cause: Repeats a number from the story.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 1 h 10 min as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw a time bar and shade what is done.

learning_experiences: use locally available materials to model Kenyan currency denominations for use in learning,
in pairs/groups, sort Kenyan currency notes according to their value up to sh.1000,
in pairs/groups, count Kenyan currency notes in different denominations up to sh1000,
in pairs/groups, subtract money up to sh.1000 in real life situations,
in pairs/groups, add money up to sh.1000 in real life situations,
in pairs/groups, role play changing money into different denominations up to sh. 1000 in the classroom model shop,
in pairs/groups, role play buying up to 3 items involving balance using the money models up to sh.1000 in the classroom model shop,
share own experiences in relation to shopping activities,
play digital games involving money.
key_inquiry_questions: How can money be represented in different denominations?
sub_strands.design_notes: Outcomes a to g are KICD's words; h is attitudinal. Kenyan notes up to sh. 1,000 (50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000) and coins (1, 5, 10, 20); all amounts within sh. 1,000; buying up to 3 items with a balance in a classroom model shop.

source.version: PDF on disk, text layer (read in place)

outcomes.text: identify Kenyan currency notes up to sh.1000
count money in different denominations up to sh.1000
add money involving different denominations up to a sh.1000
subtract money involving different denominations up to a sh.1000
represent the same amount of money in different denominations
convert money into different denominations
use money to buy up to 3 items involving balance
appreciate spending and saving money in real life situations

skills.name: Identify Kenyan currency notes up to sh. 1,000
skills.mastery: The child names the Kenyan notes of sh. 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1,000 by their value (from the number, colour and size), sorts notes by value, and tells notes from coins.

prerequisites.reason: Identifies coins and notes up to sh. 100.

skills.name: Count money in different denominations up to sh. 1,000
skills.mastery: The child counts a mix of notes and coins up to sh. 1,000 by starting with the largest and counting on in its value (500, 700, 800, 850, 870), and writes the total with sh.

skills.name: Add money up to sh. 1,000
skills.mastery: The child adds amounts of money up to sh. 1,000 (sh. 350 + sh. 275), with single regrouping, in shopping stories and in columns, and writes sh.

skills.name: Subtract money up to sh. 1,000
skills.mastery: The child subtracts amounts of money up to sh. 1,000 (what is left after spending, how much more one item costs), with single regrouping, and writes sh.

skills.name: Represent the same amount of money in different denominations
skills.mastery: The child shows one amount (sh. 200) in two or more ways (one sh. 200 note; two sh. 100 notes; four sh. 50 notes) and says whether two collections are worth the same.
question_forms: how many of a note make the amount

skills.name: Convert money into different denominations
skills.mastery: The child changes a note into smaller notes or coins (a sh. 1,000 note into sh. 500 notes, a sh. 100 note into sh. 20 coins) and says how many of the smaller kind are given.
question_forms: how many of a smaller note
what is missing in the change

prerequisites.reason: Shows an amount in different ways.

skills.name: Use money to buy up to 3 items involving balance
skills.mastery: The child finds the total cost of up to 3 items, takes it from the money paid, and gives the balance (change), within sh. 1,000, and checks that cost plus balance equals the money paid.
question_forms: role play at the model shop

prerequisites.reason: Subtracts the cost from the money paid.

misconceptions.error: Names notes by colour alone and mixes notes of similar colour.

example.question: Which note is worth sh. 500?

misconceptions.cause: Uses colour, not the number printed.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the sh. 50 note as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Read the number on each note first.

misconceptions.error: Thinks more notes always means more money, whatever their value.

example.question: Which is worth more: three sh. 50 notes or one sh. 500 note?

misconceptions.cause: Counts notes, not value.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer three sh. 50 notes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the value: 50, 100, 150.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a coin is always worth less than any note, or a big coin more than a note.

example.question: Which is worth more: a sh. 20 coin or a sh. 50 note?

misconceptions.cause: Judges by size or kind.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the sh. 20 coin as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Compare the numbers printed.

misconceptions.error: Sorts notes in the wrong order of value.

example.question: Order from least to most: sh. 1,000, sh. 50, sh. 200.

misconceptions.cause: Orders by position or colour.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 1,000, sh. 50, sh. 200 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Line them up by the number.

misconceptions.error: Counts the number of notes and coins instead of their value.

example.question: A purse has one sh. 500 note, two sh. 100 notes and one sh. 50 note. How much money?

misconceptions.cause: Counts pieces.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Start with the largest and count on in its value.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Counts on by one step for every piece, as 500, 501, 502.

example.question: Count: sh. 500 note and two sh. 100 notes.

misconceptions.cause: Counts on in ones.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 502 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count on by the value of each note.

misconceptions.error: Starts with the small coins and loses count.

example.question: Count: sh. 20, sh. 20, sh. 200, sh. 50.

misconceptions.cause: Adds in the order given and slips.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 280 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Sort first: largest to smallest, then count on.

misconceptions.error: Writes the total without sh.

example.question: Write the total of two sh. 100 notes.

misconceptions.cause: Drops the unit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 200 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Money totals always carry sh.

misconceptions.error: Forgets the carry when adding prices.
misconceptions.cause: Regrouping slip.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 525 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Add as numbers, carrying the hundred.

misconceptions.error: Subtracts when asked for the total cost.

example.question: A book costs sh. 250 and a pen sh. 30. What is the total cost?

misconceptions.cause: Takes away because one is smaller.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 220 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Total cost: add.

misconceptions.error: Lines up a 2-digit price under the hundreds.
misconceptions.cause: Lines up from the left.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 1025 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Line up from the right.

misconceptions.error: Adds only some of the items in the list.

example.question: Bread sh. 60, milk sh. 70, sugar sh. 150. Total?

misconceptions.cause: Stops after two items.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 130 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Tick each item as it is added.

misconceptions.error: Takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.
misconceptions.cause: Column error with zeros.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 425 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Open a hundred, then a ten.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds when asked how much is left.

example.question: Juma has sh. 600 and spends sh. 250. How much is left?

misconceptions.cause: Sees two numbers and adds.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 850 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Spending makes less.

misconceptions.error: Gives the amount spent as the money left.

example.question: Achieng had sh. 400 and spent sh. 150. How much is left?

misconceptions.cause: Repeats a number.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 150 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw the money and cross off what is spent.

misconceptions.error: Adds when asked how much more one item costs.

example.question: A bag costs sh. 450 and a book sh. 200. How much more is the bag?

misconceptions.cause: 'More' sounds like add.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 650 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: How much more is the gap between them.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a collection with more pieces is worth more.

example.question: Are two sh. 100 notes worth the same as one sh. 200 note?

misconceptions.cause: Counts notes.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer no, two notes are more as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the value of each collection.

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong number of the smaller note.

example.question: How many sh. 50 notes make sh. 200?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks of halving once.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count in fifties: 50, 100, 150, 200.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an amount can only be shown one way.

example.question: Show sh. 500 another way than one sh. 500 note.

misconceptions.cause: Has not seen that values can be swapped.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer cannot as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Exchange at the model shop: one note for smaller ones.

misconceptions.error: Adds the numbers on the notes wrongly when checking, as 200 + 200 + 100 = 400.

example.question: Do two sh. 200 notes and one sh. 100 note make sh. 500?

misconceptions.cause: Addition slip.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer no, sh. 400 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong number of smaller notes in exchange.

example.question: Change a sh. 1,000 note into sh. 200 notes. How many?

misconceptions.cause: Divides by the wrong number or counts in hundreds.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 10 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count in two hundreds to 1,000.

misconceptions.error: Thinks changing a note for coins loses money because coins are small.

example.question: Is a sh. 100 note changed for five sh. 20 coins a fair exchange?

misconceptions.cause: Judges value by size.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer no as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the coins' value.

misconceptions.error: Cannot find the missing part of the change.

example.question: A sh. 500 note is changed into sh. 200 and some sh. 100 notes. How many sh. 100 notes?

misconceptions.cause: Takes the 200 as two 100s twice.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.

misconceptions.error: Gives the value of each smaller note instead of how many.

example.question: How many sh. 50 notes for a sh. 100 note?

misconceptions.cause: Answers with the note's value.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 50 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.

example.question: Bread sh. 60 and milk sh. 70, paid with sh. 200. Change?

misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 130 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Balance is money paid minus cost.

example.question: Bread sh. 60 and milk sh. 70, paid with sh. 200. Change?

misconceptions.cause: Forgets the other item.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 140 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Add all the items first.

example.question: A ball costs sh. 350. Paid with sh. 500. Change?

misconceptions.cause: Adds the two numbers.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer sh. 850 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.

in pairs/groups, play a game of moving to the right and left sides from a point,

turn to the left from a point

skills.name: Move along a straight line from a point
skills.mastery: The child moves (or moves a counter on a grid) a given number of steps along a straight line from a stated starting point, forwards or backwards, and says where they end up and how many steps they moved.
question_forms: where do you end after the steps
how many steps from the start
move forward or back on a path
skills.hands_on: Moving along lines outside the classroom is done in class.

skills.name: Identify the right and left side from a point
skills.mastery: The child says which objects are on their right and left, and on the right or left of a person facing them or facing another way, using the person's own right and left.
question_forms: right or left of the person in the picture

prerequisites.reason: Moves from a point, so has a facing direction.
Identifies objects and shapes in the environment.

skills.name: Turn to the right or to the left from a point
skills.mastery: The child moves straight from a point, turns a quarter turn to the right or the left, and says what they now face or which way they now go; in pictures and on paths, they follow a route of moves and turns.
question_forms: what do you face after turning right
turn left or right to reach a place

misconceptions.error: Counts the starting square as the first step.

example.question: A counter is on square 3 of a straight path. It moves 4 steps forward. Where is it?

misconceptions.cause: Says 'one' on the square it starts on.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 6 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count only when the counter lands on a new square.

misconceptions.error: Moves backwards when told forwards, or the reverse.

example.question: Start at the tree and walk 5 steps back towards the gate. Are you nearer the tree or the gate?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes forward and back.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the tree as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Point the way before moving.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a bending path is a straight line.

example.question: Is a path round a flower bed a straight line?

misconceptions.cause: Calls any path a line.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A straight line does not bend: check with a stretched string.

misconceptions.error: Counts steps from the wrong starting point.

example.question: From the door, Amina walks 6 steps to the desk. From the desk she walks 3 more. How many steps from the door?

misconceptions.cause: Counts only the last move.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Mark the starting point and add every move from it.

misconceptions.error: Gives his own right for the right of a person facing him.

example.question: Kamau faces you and raises his right hand. Is it on your right or your left?

misconceptions.cause: Uses his own body, not Kamau's.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer my right as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Stand beside the person, facing the same way.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up right and left on their own body.

example.question: Hold up your left hand.

misconceptions.cause: Has not fixed the names.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer right hand as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The left hand makes an L with thumb and finger.

misconceptions.error: Uses the viewer's left and right for a person in a picture facing out.

example.question: A boy in a picture faces you. A ball is by his right hand. Which side of the page is it on?

misconceptions.cause: Reads the page sides as the boy's sides.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the right side as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Turn the picture: what would the boy's right be?

misconceptions.error: Answers front or behind when asked right or left.

example.question: What is on your right when you face the board?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes facing with sides.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the board as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Right and left are the sides, not the front.

misconceptions.error: Turns left when told to turn right.

example.question: You face the gate and turn right. Do you face the side with the office or the side with the field (office on your right)?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes the names when turning.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the field as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Raise the right hand, then turn to face where it points.

misconceptions.error: Makes a half turn, ending up facing back.

example.question: You face the board and turn right. Do you face the back wall?

misconceptions.cause: Turns too far.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A turn to the right is a quarter turn: only to the side.

misconceptions.error: In a route, makes each turn from the first facing, not the new one.

example.question: Walk forward, turn right, walk, turn right again. Which way do you face now?
example.wrong_answer: the same as after the first turn

misconceptions.cause: Forgets that turning changes the facing.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer the same as after the first turn as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Act it out; after each turn your right is new.

misconceptions.error: Steps sideways instead of turning the body.

example.question: Turn left: do you step to the left side, or turn to face it?

misconceptions.cause: Reads turn as move.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer step sideways as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Keep your feet on the spot and turn your body.

learning_experiences: in pairs/groups, make paper cut-out of different shapes,
in pairs or groups, sort out the paper cut-outs according to their shapes,
in pairs or groups, name the different shapes made from the paper cut-outs,
in pairs/groups, name and discuss shapes in their immediate environment,
in pairs/groups, draw combined shapes found in the environment that are made of 2 different shapes, e.g. the hut,
in groups, use locally available materials to model a combined shape made of 2 different shapes,
play digital games involving shapes.
key_inquiry_questions: What shapes can you identify in your school?
sub_strands.design_notes: Outcomes a to c are KICD's words; d is attitudinal. Combined shapes are made of two different shapes (a hut is a triangle on a rectangle). Drawing and modelling are done with paper cut-outs and local materials in class.

source.version: PDF on disk, text layer (read in place)

outcomes.text: identify the shapes in a combined shape made of two different shapes
draw a combined shape made of 2 shapes
model a combined shape made of two shapes
appreciate the use of combined shapes in the environment

skills.name: Name the basic shapes: rectangle, square, triangle, circle and oval
skills.mastery: The child names a rectangle, a square, a triangle, a circle and an oval from cut-outs, drawings and objects, in any position or size, by their sides and corners (a triangle has 3 sides), not by how they are turned.
question_forms: find the shape in an object

skills.name: Identify the shapes in a combined shape made of two different shapes
skills.mastery: Given a combined shape (a hut, a house, an ice cream cone) the child names the two shapes it is made of and points to where one ends and the other begins.
question_forms: name the top and bottom shape
which picture is a triangle and a square

skills.name: Draw a combined shape made of two shapes
skills.mastery: The child draws a combined shape of two named shapes (a triangle on top of a square for a house), with the shapes sharing an edge and each shape drawn with the right number of sides.

prerequisites.reason: Sees the two shapes in a combined shape.

skills.hands_on: Drawing combined shapes is done in class, with the teacher checking the drawings.

skills.name: Model a combined shape made of two shapes
skills.mastery: The child makes a combined shape of two shapes from paper cut-outs, sticks or clay (a rectangle and a triangle for a hut) and names the two parts.

prerequisites.reason: Knows which shapes make the model.

skills.hands_on: Modelling with local materials is done in class.

misconceptions.error: Calls a square turned on its corner a diamond and says it is not a square.

example.question: A square is turned so a corner points up. Is it still a square?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks turning changes the shape.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer no, a diamond as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Turn a square cut-out and count its equal sides.
misconceptions.source: widely reported in maths-education research; how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls an oval a circle.

example.question: An egg shape: circle or oval?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks every round shape is a circle.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer circle as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A circle is the same across every way; an oval is longer one way.

misconceptions.error: Calls a long rectangle a square, or a square a triangle, by counting corners wrongly.

example.question: A shape has 4 sides: 2 long and 2 short. What is it?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks every 4-sided shape is a square.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer square as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A square has 4 equal sides; a rectangle has 2 long and 2 short.

misconceptions.error: Says a triangle standing on its point, or a long thin one, is not a triangle.

example.question: A shape with 3 straight sides points down. Is it a triangle?

misconceptions.cause: Has only seen triangles standing on a base.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer no as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the sides: any 3-sided shape is a triangle.

misconceptions.error: Sees the combined shape as one new shape and cannot name its parts.

example.question: A hut drawing: which two shapes make it?

misconceptions.cause: Sees the object, not the shapes.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer a hut as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Cover the top: what shape is left? Then cover the bottom.

misconceptions.error: Counts all the outside sides and names a shape with that many sides.

example.question: A triangle on a square makes a house. Which two shapes?

misconceptions.cause: Counts the outline.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer a pentagon as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Look for the line inside that splits the two shapes.

misconceptions.error: Names one shape twice, as two triangles for a cone.

example.question: An ice cream cone: which two shapes?

misconceptions.cause: Names the shape seen first for both parts.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer two triangles as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Point to each part on its own and name it.

misconceptions.error: Names the parts by their use (roof, door) instead of their shape.

example.question: What shape is the roof of the hut drawing?

misconceptions.cause: Answers with the object's name.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer roof as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask 'what shape?', not 'what is it?'

misconceptions.error: Draws the two shapes apart instead of joined.

example.question: Draw a triangle on top of a square to make a house. Are the shapes touching?

misconceptions.cause: Draws the two shapes separately.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer drawn apart as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw the square first, then use its top side as the triangle's base.

misconceptions.error: Draws one of the parts with the wrong number of sides.

example.question: Draw a rectangle with a triangle on it. How many sides does your triangle have?

misconceptions.cause: Draws freehand without counting.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the sides as you draw.

misconceptions.error: Draws curved sides for a shape with straight sides.

example.question: Draw a hut: square walls and triangle roof. Are your lines straight?

misconceptions.cause: Draws quickly without a ruler.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer curved as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Use a ruler for straight sides.

misconceptions.error: Adds a third shape, so it is no longer made of two.

example.question: Draw a combined shape of two shapes: a rectangle and a triangle.

misconceptions.cause: Decorates the drawing.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer rectangle, triangle and circle as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Count the shapes in your drawing.

misconceptions.error: Picks a cut-out of the wrong shape for one part.

example.question: Model a hut with a rectangle and a triangle. Which pieces?

misconceptions.cause: Picks by colour or size.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer a rectangle and a circle as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Name each piece before using it.

misconceptions.error: Lays the pieces apart instead of joining them along a side.

example.question: Is a triangle placed far from a rectangle a combined shape?

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that the parts must share an edge.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Slide the pieces until a side touches.

misconceptions.error: Overlaps the pieces so one shape is hidden.

example.question: If the triangle covers half the rectangle, can you still see both shapes?

misconceptions.cause: Puts one piece on top of the other.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put the pieces side by side, edges touching.

misconceptions.error: Names the model as the object only and not its two shapes.

example.question: What shapes is your model made of?

misconceptions.cause: Answers with the object.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer a house as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask: which shapes did you use?
